concept.body: Perpendicular lines have slopes multiplying to −1 (negative reciprocals) — proved by rotating a slope triangle 90°: displacement (a, b) becomes (−b, a), and (b/a)(−a/b) = −1. One exception: vertical lines (undefined slope) are perpendicular to horizontal ones — test that pair separately.

widget.prompt: A line has slope 4. Perpendicular slope (decimal) = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 0.25 flips without negating — the product must be −1: −0.25.
−4 negates without flipping — (4)(−4) = −16: the perpendicular is −1/4 = −0.25.

steps.body: The perpendicular rule — slopes multiply to −1 — falls to a **quarter-turn**. Rotate a slope triangle 90° about its corner (a rigid motion): the run (a, 0) turns into a rise, the rise (0, b) into a LEFTWARD run — displacement (a, b) becomes (−b, a). New slope: a/(−b). Old times new: (b/a)(−a/b) = **−1**, always.

widget.prompt: A line has slope 2/3. Enter the slope of a perpendicular line (as a decimal).

commonErrors.feedback: 0.67 copies the slope — that's the PARALLEL rule. Perpendicular flips and negates: −3/2 = −1.5.
1.5 flips without negating — the product must be −1: −1.5.
−0.67 negates without flipping — (2/3)(−2/3) = −4/9 ≠ −1. The full move: −3/2 = −1.5.

explanationVariants: Slope BA = 2/3 and slope BC = (6 − 3)/(2 − 4) = −3/2: product −1 — right angle at B. Enter −1.5.

widget.prompt: A(1, 1), B(4, 3), C(2, 6). Compute slope BC (decimal) — then multiply by slope AB (2/3) in your head.

commonErrors.feedback: 1.5 drops the sign — x DECREASES from B to C (4 → 2): 3/(−2) = −1.5, and the product with 2/3 is −1: right angle.
3 is the rise alone — the run is −2: slope −1.5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Slope BC = −1.5; (2/3)(−1.5) = −1 ⇒ the angle at B is right — a protractor-free proof.

steps.body: Care at the edges: the rule serves every pair EXCEPT when one line is vertical — vertical lines have no slope, yet they're perpendicular to every horizontal (slope 0) line. A complete perpendicularity test: slopes multiply to −1, OR one is vertical and the other horizontal. Coordinate proofs must remember the exception.

explanationVariants: x = 3 is vertical (undefined slope); y = −2 is horizontal (slope 0). Product test fails to apply — yet they're perpendicular.
Vertical-horizontal: the one perpendicular pair the −1 rule can't see.

options.label: Yes: vertical and horizontal are perpendicular
options.feedback: x = 3 has UNDEFINED slope, so no product exists — the complete test carries this pair as its explicit exception.

options.label: No: they lack a slope product of −1
options.feedback: The product is UNDEFINED, not ≠ −1 — and the lines visibly cross at a right angle at (3, −2).

options.label: Only if their intersection is the origin
options.feedback: They cross at (3, −2), and perpendicularity doesn't care where — vertical ⊥ horizontal, always.

options.label: No: the two lines have parallel directions
options.feedback: Parallel lines never meet — these cross at (3, −2), and at a right angle.

widget.prompt: The proof rotates the slope triangle 90°. What exactly does the rotation deliver?

choices.label: A line guaranteed perpendicular to the original, whose slope we can READ from the rotated displacement (−b, a)
choices.feedback: The 90° rotation manufactures perpendicularity by definition; the coordinate rule (a, b) → (−b, a) then hands us the new slope to compare.

choices.label: It proves the two triangles are congruent by SSS
choices.feedback: They ARE congruent (rigid motion), but the payoff is the perpendicular DIRECTION plus its readable slope a/(−b).

choices.label: It shows all slopes equal −1
choices.feedback: Slopes vary freely — it's the PRODUCT of the pair that locks at −1.

choices.label: Nothing — rotations don't preserve lines
choices.feedback: Rotations are rigid motions: lines to lines, lengths kept — exactly why the argument is airtight.

widget.successFeedback: The 90° rotation manufactures perpendicularity by definition; the coordinate rule (a, b) → (−b, a) then hands us the new slope to compare.
widget.explorationFeedback: Open at least two coordinate-proof states before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Inspect the coordinate invariants, then choose the supported conclusion.

widget.prompt: A triangle has base from (0, 0) to (8, 4). Compute the slope of the ALTITUDE dropped onto that base (decimal).

commonErrors.feedback: 0.5 is the BASE's slope — the altitude runs perpendicular: −2.
2 flips 1/2 but keeps the sign — negate too: (1/2)(−2) = −1 ✓.

hints: The perpendicular through B(6, 4) to a slope-2/3 line has slope −3/2.
explanationVariants: Two negatives make the climb positive: 13.

widget.prompt: A line through B(6, 4) is PERPENDICULAR to a slope-2/3 line. Find its y-value at x = 0.

commonErrors.feedback: 0 rides the PARALLEL slope 2/3: 4 + (2/3)(−6) = 0. Perpendicular takes −3/2: y = 13.
9 is the RISE alone — add the starting height: 4 + 9 = 13.

takeaways: Rotating (a, b) to (−b, a) proves perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
Complete test: product −1, OR vertical-meets-horizontal (the undefined exception).
Right angles, altitudes, and axis intercepts all fall to slope arithmetic — no protractor.
